notes.meaning: A young woman lies on her bed at night, longing for the man she loves, but discovers he is not there. In traditional Christian teaching, this describes a believer or the church feeling a painful sense that Christ is absent. Times of spiritual dryness remind believers how much they need the Lord's presence and spur them to seek Him more earnestly.

Troubled by his absence, the woman resolves to get up and search the streets and public squares of the city. She searches everywhere, yet she still cannot find him. Traditionally, this shows a believer leaving spiritual ease behind to seek Christ through prayer and public worship, even though the comfort of His presence is not always felt right away.

During her search, the woman meets the city watchmen who patrol the streets and guard the walls at night. She immediately asks if they have seen the one she loves, but they are unable to give her an answer. In traditional thought, these watchmen picture church ministers, who can guide seekers in the right direction but cannot take the place of Christ Himself.

Right after leaving the watchmen, she finally finds the one she loves and clings to him tightly so he cannot leave. She brings him to her mother's home, showing that she seeks an honorable, public marriage. Traditionally, this represents the soul laying hold of Christ by faith and bringing Him into the heart and the fellowship of the church.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic commentators have traditionally seen this verse as picturing Mary Magdalene clinging to the risen Jesus on the morning of the resurrection.

notes.meaning: Having found her beloved, the maiden warns the young women of Jerusalem not to interrupt their peaceful rest. Love is precious and gentle, and it must not be forced before the right time arrives. In Christian devotion, this urges believers to avoid sin and carelessness so that nothing disrupts their close, quiet communion with Christ.

Onlookers see a royal procession traveling up from the desert toward Jerusalem. Clouds of perfumed smoke rise into the air from burning myrrh and frankincense, making the procession look like pillars of smoke. In traditional teaching, this portrays the church being led out of the wilderness of the world, rising toward God with prayers and pure devotions.

The procession includes King Solomon's royal traveling carriage, surrounded by sixty of Israel's bravest warriors. The king provides full safety and honor for his bride on her journey. Traditionally, this shows that Christ surrounds His people with His mighty power, keeping the church completely safe from spiritual enemies.

Every guard in the escort is a seasoned soldier, carrying a sword on his hip to fight off night attacks from bandits or wild beasts. These men are fully prepared for sudden alarms during the journey. In the traditional view, this points to spiritual watchfulness and the Word of God protecting believers through the dark trials of this earthly life.

King Solomon constructed this grand royal carriage from the fine cedar wood of Lebanon. Cedar was prized across the ancient world for its pleasant fragrance, strength, and resistance to rot. Traditionally, this chariot represents the gospel message, built by Christ to safely carry His believers to their heavenly home.

The carriage has silver posts, a solid gold base, and cushions covered in royal purple fabric. Its interior was lovingly decorated by the women of Jerusalem as a token of honor and joy. In Christian interpretation, these rich materials represent the precious, pure promises of God, which are lined with His deep love for His people.

The young women of the city are called to come out and admire King Solomon wearing his wedding crown. This special crown was placed on his head by his mother, Bathsheba, on the day of his wedding celebration. Traditionally, this invites all people of faith to behold Christ the King, who rejoices over His redeemed church as a bridegroom rejoices over his bride.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic tradition often connects the crown given by Christ's mother to His human nature received from Mary, or to the crown of thorns placed on Him during His passion.
